summary: Proposes extensions to TLS so it can use OpenPGP keys instead of X.509 certificates, including negotiating the certificate type and changes to the handshake. It is an experimental protocol and was replaced by RFC 6091.

eli5.summary: This lets a secure web connection use a different kind of ID card, the type used by email-encryption people. It was replaced by RFC 6091.

questions: how to negotiate certificate types in tls
subtitle: TLS can authenticate using OpenPGP keys instead of X.509 certificates.

tldr.problem: TLS only supported X.509 certificates at the time, but some users wanted to use OpenPGP keys for authentication instead.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds a certificate type extension to TLS that lets peers negotiate the use of OpenPGP keys during the handshake, with changes to how certificates are sent and validated.
tldr.outcome: The protocol allows TLS connections to use OpenPGP keys, offering compatibility with an alternative certificate format. It was superseded by RFC 6091.

today: RFC 5081 is an experimental RFC that was superseded by RFC 6091. The later specification provides a more mature approach to integrating OpenPGP keys into TLS.

sections.title: Introduction to OpenPGP Authentication
sections.content:
Transport Layer Security (TLS) is the protocol that secures web connections and other internet applications. Historically, TLS has used X.509 certificates for authentication. However, the OpenPGP standard defines a different certificate format used widely by email encryption tools. This RFC proposes extensions to TLS so it can authenticate using OpenPGP keys instead of X.509 certificates.

The extension is backward compatible: TLS implementations that only support X.509 certificates are unaffected. Both client and server can negotiate which certificate type to use during the TLS handshake.
sections.eli5: Imagine TLS (secure connections) usually uses one kind of ID. This adds the ability to use a different ID that email programs already know about.

sections.title: Negotiating the Certificate Type
sections.content:
The client and server agree on which certificate type to use by adding a new extension to the TLS handshake. During the client hello, the client lists the certificate types it supports. If the client only supports X.509, it omits this extension entirely, maintaining backward compatibility. The server responds in its hello message with the single certificate type it chooses to use.

The negotiation process mirrors the way TLS negotiates cipher suites, ensuring the same security properties apply. If the server cannot provide a certificate in the type the client wants, it terminates the connection with an error.
sections.eli5: During the secret handshake when a connection starts, they agree on what kind of ID to use. If both like X.509, great. If one wants OpenPGP and the server can do it, they use that.

sections.title: OpenPGP Certificate Formats
sections.content:
When OpenPGP is negotiated, certificates are sent in OpenPGP binary format. The RFC requires that OpenPGP certificates contain all elements required by the OpenPGP specification, including the public key and any user identity information.

The sender also has the option to send only an OpenPGP fingerprint (a 16 to 20 byte cryptographic hash) instead of the entire certificate. If the peer cannot find a certificate matching that fingerprint, it responds with an alert. This saves bandwidth when both sides already have the certificate.
sections.eli5: An OpenPGP ID is sent as-is in its own format. Optionally, instead of sending the whole thing, you can send just its fingerprint if the other side already has a copy.

sections.title: Changes to the TLS Handshake
sections.content:
Most TLS handshake messages stay the same. The certificate message works differently when OpenPGP is negotiated: the peer sends either a complete OpenPGP certificate or just its fingerprint. The certificate request message (used when the server asks for client authentication) remains the same, but the authority list MUST be empty because OpenPGP does not use certificate chains in the same way X.509 does.

The client sends its certificate in response to a certificate request using the same format as the server: either the full certificate or the fingerprint. If the client has no certificate available, it sends an empty certificate vector rather than failing.
sections.eli5: The handshake mostly stays the same. When certificates are swapped, they use the OpenPGP format. Everything else about how TLS works stays normal.

sections.title: Security Properties
sections.content:
The security analysis relies on the security properties of TLS and OpenPGP themselves. The certificate type negotiation provides the same security as TLS's cipher suite negotiation because both use the same underlying mechanisms and protection. The use of fingerprints instead of full certificates is safe when used appropriately, since an OpenPGP fingerprint serves as a cryptographic hash.

Questions about the validity of an OpenPGP certificate (such as whether it belongs to whom it claims, or whether it should be trusted) are outside the scope of this specification and are handled by the application layer or the user. The protocol simply provides the mechanism to exchange and use these keys.
sections.eli5: Since OpenPGP and TLS are already secure on their own, using them together is as safe as using them separately. The application decides whether to trust someone.

sections.title: Implementation and Status
sections.content:
This RFC defined an experimental protocol, and its use was limited in practice. The specification defined a TLS extension with the value 9 in the TLS ExtensionType registry, and created a registry for certificate types with values 0 (X.509) and 1 (OpenPGP). Future values could be assigned through IETF consensus, and values 224 through 255 were reserved for private use.

RFC 6091 later superseded this work with an improved approach. While this RFC provided a working mechanism to use OpenPGP keys in TLS, the later standard better integrated OpenPGP support into the TLS ecosystem.
sections.eli5: This was an early attempt at letting TLS use OpenPGP keys. A later version did it better, so this one is not used anymore.
